title: How I learned to stop worrying and love StopGrads: Stationarity, Convergence, and a case study on Flow Map Learning

paper.title: How I learned to stop worrying and love StopGrads: Stationarity, Convergence, and a case study on Flow Map Learning
paper.abstract:
Abstract Stopgrads are widely used in training machine learning models, but stopgrads can alter the gradient, stationary points and convergence guarantees of the original objective, which can make stopgrad training theoretically ungrounded. We introduce a stopgrad regression principle , which identifies a general template for stopgrad objectives with a closed-form characterization of stationary points and their uniqueness, unifying stopgrad objectives for flow maps, reinforcement learning, and diffusion samplers.
We provide theoretical grounding for optimizing stopgrad flow map objectives by showing their unique stationary point is the true flow map, and showing positive convergence results for Eulerian and Lagrangian objectives, including MeanFlow and improved MeanFlow.
Remarkably, we show that under functional semi-gradient flow, the learned flow map has a closed-form expression composing the initial flow map and the true flow map.
We additionally use our stopgrad regression principle to propose modified stopgrad placements for flow map objectives which reduce training memory by 2 × 2\times .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Stop gradients ( stopgrad ) are a basic primitive in automatic differentiation packages like PyTorch and JAX. Stopgrads leave the forward pass unchanged, but in the backward pass, they return a zero gradient and block further gradient propagation. Stopgrads are widely used in machine learning, including in self-referential objectives where a model is supervised in terms of itself, as in self-distillation, reinforcement learning ( rl ) [ 43 ] , consistency models and flow maps [ 40 , 15 ] , representation learning [ 33 ] , as well as variational inference [ 35 , 45 ] . For example, in rl , popular algorithms such as temporal-difference learning and actor-critic methods rely on stopgrads in practice [ 29 , 25 , 39 , 42 ] . However, stopgrad objectives update models with semi-gradients (differentiating only some occurrences of the model), which are not the gradient of the original objective [ 42 ] . Semi-gradient update fields may be non-conservative, meaning they may not be the gradient of any objective, and updates could follow a loop indefinitely without making progress. Whereas standard gradient descent is akin to marching through mountains and valleys, optimizing stopgrad objectives can be like wandering in Escher landscapes (Fig. 1 ). These concerns motivate understanding stopgrad optimization theory, which seeks to understand the stationary points and convergence of stopgrad objectives. Figure 1 : Gradient and non-gradient update fields. Left: Gradient fields are familiar valleys and mountains, while in stopgrad update fields, learning can make no progress and may not converge ( Relativity, M.C. Escher ). Right: (a) A well-behaved gradient field. (b, c) Non-gradient fields can result from stopgrads. While (b) still has a stable stationary point at the minimum, (c) has an unstable stationary point; small perturbations move trajectories away from the minimum and toward the limit cycle. In this work, we study a class of loss functions and stopgrad placements that yield update fields that converge to desired stationary points. Recently, stopgrads have featured prominently in methods for training flow maps , which learn to integrate probability-flow ODEs in few steps [ 40 , 41 , 28 , 21 , 37 , 8 , 36 ] . MeanFlow [ 15 ] introduced a stopgrad objective but did not analyze its stationary points or convergence. Boffi et al. [8] , Boffi et al. [9] introduced the Eulerian self-distillation ( esd ) and Lagrangian self-distillation ( lsd ) objectives and proposed specific stopgrad placements; they show the non-stopgrad loss has a unique minimum, but did not characterize the stationary points or convergence of the stopgrad variants. Despite the ubiquity and empirical utility of stopgrads, no general theoretical grounding exists for stopgrad objectives. This paper formalizes stopgrads via the calculus of variations (§ 2 ) and studies the stationary points and convergence of stopgrad objectives. Concretely, the paper makes the following contributions: ⋆ \star We introduce a stopgrad regression principle (§ 3 ), a general template for stopgrad objectives with a closed-form characterization of its stationary points as fixed points of the target operator. The template describes objectives where the learned model appears once outside the stopgrad, and regresses against targets that are affine in labels and stopgrad terms of the learned model. We also give a sufficient condition on the target operator under which a unique attainable minimizer of the ordinary (non-stopgrad) loss is the unique stationary point of the stopgrad loss, and we prove uniqueness directly for each flow map objective. The stopgrad regression principle is general, encompassing stopgrad objectives for flow maps, rl , and diffusion samplers [ 19 ] . The principle’s template is easy to check, so it assists in the design of new stopgrad objectives. ⋆ \star We apply the stopgrad regression principle to MeanFlow with stopgrad, and show that the true flow map is its unique stationary point , as desired. In contrast, removing the stopgrad removes the true flow map as a stationary point [ 8 ] , showing that the stopgrad in MeanFlow is necessary for principled optimization (§ 4.1 ). ⋆ \star We show that the true flow map is the unique stationary point of improved MeanFlow (§ 4.2 ). ⋆ \star We derive two new stopgrad objectives by introducing stopgrads in placements prescribed by the regression principle template in the ESD and LSD flow map objectives (§ 4.3 - 4.4 ), without changing the unique stationarity of the true flow map. We call these slim esd and lsd , as our stopgrads reduce training memory by 2 × 2\times . Concurrent work has proposed equivalent objectives [ 22 , 34 ] , whereas we derive them in a principled manner from stopgrad optimization perspectives. We train flow maps and show that slim esd and lsd match or improve on Fréchet inception distance ( fid ) on cifar-10 and ImageNet . ⋆ \star We show positive convergence results for MeanFlow, Improved MeanFlow ( imf ) , slim esd , slim lsd (§ 5 ). We verify that their semi-gradients are not gradients of any objective, which raises questions on convergence. For slim esd , lsd , and imf , we study convergence of distillation training following perfect flow-matching pretraining, whereas we study MeanFlow training from scratch. Remarkably, we show that under functional semi-gradient flow, the learned flow map is a closed-form composition of the initial flow map and the true flow map , with “hand-off time” varying with optimization time (Fig. 2 ). Under standard assumptions, convergence occurs exponentially fast. Figure 2 : Convergence via closed-form composition (§ 5 ). Under functional semi-gradient flow, the learned flow map F τ F_{\tau} at optimization time τ \tau is a composition of the initial F 0 F_{0} and the true flow map F ∗ F^{*} . As optimization time τ \tau passes, the “hand-off” time r τ r_{\tau} interpolates towards u u for Eulerian and t t for Lagrangian, giving convergence to the true flow map.

sections.heading: 2 Stopgrads in ML: from PyTorch to Proofs
sections.text: We formalize a mathematical definition of the stopgrad operator that is consistent with what is computed in practice. We start with stopgrads computed in programming libraries, move to directional derivatives, and then generalize to functional derivatives, which form the basis of our results.

sections.heading: 3 Stopgrad Regression Principle
sections.text: Here, we present a unifying stopgrad regression principle. This principle identifies a general template for stopgrad objectives where the learned function appears in only one term outside of stopgrads, though it can appear within stopgrads in multiple terms. When the stopgrad-ed operator takes a certain affine form, our stopgrad regression principle characterizes the stationary points as the fixed points of the target operator. Whether that fixed point is unique is a separate question: we give a sufficient condition in Corollary 1 , and establish uniqueness for each flow map objective in § 4 . In particular, if ℒ \mathcal{L} attains the value V V at exactly one f ∗ ∈ ℳ f^{*}\in\mathcal{M} , then f ∗ f^{*} is the unique stationary point of ℒ \mathcal{L} in ℳ \mathcal{M} . sections.heading: Connection to fixed-point iteration
sections.text: In reinforcement learning, the value function is the fixed point of the Bellman operator [ 4 , 42 , 5 ] in the td( 0 ) row of Table 1 . How does this relate to stop-gradient regression? Taking the semi-gradient of the stop-gradient regression and applying a unit step yields f ← f − ( f − T ⁡ [ f , 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝐲 | 𝐱 ] ] ) = T ⁡ [ f , 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝐲 | 𝐱 ] ] f\;\leftarrow\;f-(f-T[f,\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}]])\;=\;T[f,\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}]] which is exactly fixed-point iteration of T T . The update vanishes precisely when f = T ⁡ [ f ] f=T[f] , so the zeros of the semi-gradient coincide with the fixed-point of T T by construction. In the rl case, this fixed point is the desired value function, and it is unique because the Bellman operator is a γ \gamma -contraction for γ < 1 \gamma<1 [ 38 , 7 , 12 ] (§ D ). Our perspective highlights that this equivalence is not specific to Bellman iteration: semi-gradient updates of stop-gradient regression implement fixed-point iteration of the underlying operator, including for problems not typically framed in fixed-point terms, such as partial differential equation ( pde ) -based flow-map loss functionals. sections.heading: 4 Stationary Points of Stopgrad Flow Map Objectives
sections.text: Flow maps learn to sample probability flow ordinary differential equations ( odes ) in few steps, and are trained with objectives involving stopgrad operators. We now analyze the stationary points of these stopgrad flow map objectives. We begin by reviewing background.

sections.heading: Stochastic Interpolants
sections.text: Given simple 𝐱 0 ∼ q 0 \mathbf{x}_{0}\sim q_{0} and data 𝐱 1 ∼ q 1 \mathbf{x}_{1}\sim q_{1} , stochastic interpolants [ 26 , 1 ] define a density path by constructing 𝐱 t = α t ​ 𝐱 0 + σ t ​ 𝐱 1 \mathbf{x}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\,\mathbf{x}_{0}+\sigma_{t}\,\mathbf{x}_{1} , for t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] . Under this construction, there exists a velocity field v ⁡ ( t , x ) := 𝔼 [ 𝐱 ˙ t | 𝐱 t = x ] v(t,x):=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[\dot{\mathbf{x}}_{t}~|~\mathbf{x}_{t}=x] with 𝐱 ˙ t = α ˙ t ​ 𝐱 0 + σ ˙ t ​ 𝐱 1 \dot{\mathbf{x}}_{t}=\dot{\alpha}_{t}\mathbf{x}_{0}+\dot{\sigma}_{t}\mathbf{x}_{1} , such that the ode d ​ 𝐱 ^ t = v ⁡ ( t , 𝐱 ^ t ) ​ d ​ t d\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t}=v(t,\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\,dt has the same marginal densities as 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} . The ode connection provides a way to sample the marginals of 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} while only having access to a sample of one endpoint and the velocity field v v . In practice, v v is learned by regressing a model v θ v_{\theta} against 𝐱 ˙ t \dot{\mathbf{x}}_{t} via the so-called flow-matching loss 𝔼 [ ‖ v θ ​ ( t , 𝐱 t ) − 𝐱 ˙ t ‖ 2 ] \mathop{\mathbb{E}}[\|v_{\theta}(t,\mathbf{x}_{t})-\dot{\mathbf{x}}_{t}\|^{2}] , and new samples are generated by discretizing the ode .

sections.heading: Flow maps and the transport equation
sections.text: Instead of learning v θ v_{\theta} and then integrating it in an ode , one can sample by approximating the flow map F F : F ⁡ ( t , u , 𝐱 ^ t ) := 𝐱 ^ t + ∫ t u v ⁡ ( s , 𝐱 ^ s ) ​ 𝑑 s = 𝐱 ^ t + ∫ t u v ⁡ ( s , F ⁡ ( t , s , 𝐱 ^ t ) ) ​ 𝑑 s . \displaystyle F(t,u,\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t}):=\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t}+\int_{t}^{u}v(s,\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{s})ds=\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t}+\int_{t}^{u}v(s,F(t,s,\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))ds. (12) The flow map F F describes where a particle at position x x at time t t reaches by time u u when integrated along the probability flow ode trajectories. Learning F F directly enables few-step sampling [ 40 , 21 , 8 , 9 , 41 , 15 ] . The flow map is characterized by a transport equation , which is a pde acquired by using the Leibniz rule to take the time derivative of eq. 12 : ∂ t F ⁡ ( t , u , x ) + ( ∂ x F ) ​ ( t , u , x ) ​ v ​ ( t , x ) = 0 , F ⁡ ( u , u , x ) = x . \displaystyle\partial_{t}F(t,u,x)+(\partial_{x}F)(t,u,x)\,v(t,x)=0,\qquad F(u,u,x)=x. (13) The boundary condition says that a particle at position x x at time u u is already at its destination; it is satisfied automatically when parameterizing flow maps as F ⁡ ( t , u , x ) = x + ( u − t ) ​ f ​ ( t , u , x ) . \displaystyle F(t,u,x)=x+(u-t)\,f(t,u,x). (14) Rewriting ( 13 ) in terms of this f f parameterization gives: f = v + ( u − t ) ​ ( ∂ t f + ( ∂ x f ) ​ v ) . \displaystyle f=v+(u-t)\big(\partial_{t}f+(\partial_{x}f)\,v\big). (15) Flow-map training procedures are built from this identity and related rewritings. In practice, these methods often use stopgrads to avoid differentiating through model derivatives. In this work, we seek to understand what these stopgrads preserve and when their induced dynamics remain well behaved. In our flow map analyses, we assume regularity conditions (Remark 1 ), such as Lipschitz marginal velocities and square-integrable conditional velocities used in prior work [ 27 ] .

sections.heading: Stationary points of flow map training with stopgrads.
sections.text: For MeanFlow and improved MeanFlow, we prove the true flow map is the unique stationary point with stopgrads. For lsd and esd , the original stopgrad placements do not fit Theorem 1 , so it is not obvious what their stationary points are. Theorem 1 inspires our slim stopgrad placements that yield known stationary points and reduce training memory by avoiding second-order derivatives. In each case Theorem 1 supplies the characterization of stationary points, and uniqueness of the true flow map is proved separately (§ C ) by reducing the stationarity equation to the transport equation ( 13 ) or the flow ode and invoking uniqueness of their solutions. Throughout this section the time sampler satisfies t ≤ u t\leq u . We write Ω := { 0 < t ≤ u < 1 } × ℝ d \Omega:=\{0<t\leq u<1\}\times\mathbb{R}^{d} for the time triangle including the diagonal { t = u } \{t=u\} . The training distribution μ \mu of ( t , u , 𝐱 t ) (t,u,\mathbf{x}_{t}) has full support on the interior { t < u } \{t<u\} of Ω \Omega and may also place mass on the diagonal; Remark 1 states the precise conditions, and a glossary of symbols is in the appendix.

Substituting this into u ≠ t u\neq t , we get the transport equation ( 13 ) with F ⁡ ( u , u , x ) = x F(u,u,x)=x , so the true flow map is the unique stationary point of ℒ iMF \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{iMF}} in ℳ \mathcal{M} . sections.heading: 5 Convergence of Functional Semi-Gradient Flow for Flow Map Objectives
sections.text: It is well known that standard gradient descent converges to stationary points under standard smoothness and step-size conditions [ 20 ] . Without stopgrads, the functional gradient g g likewise defines a descent direction (when − g ⁡ [ f ] ∈ 𝒟 -g[f]\in\mathcal{D} ), and flowing along it brings optimization to a stationary point in function space. However, for stopgrad objectives which have semi-gradient update fields, it is not obvious whether following the semi-gradient field arrives at a stationary point or not. Thus, our preceding characterization of stationary points for stopgrad flow map objectives must be paired with an analysis of convergence. Here we show two things. First, semi-gradients are generally not gradients of any scalar objective; we confirm this concretely for MeanFlow, imf , slim- lsd , and slim- esd , so standard optimization theory does not guarantee their convergence. Second, despite this, functional semi-gradient flow does converge for MeanFlow, imf , slim- lsd , and slim- esd .

sections.heading: 5.1 When is a semi-gradient the gradient of an objective?
sections.text: A natural question is, when is the semi-gradient g g also the gradient of some scalar functional J : ℳ → ℝ J:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R} —equivalently, whether g g is a conservative vector field on ℳ \mathcal{M} . Knowing that g g is a gradient of some J J would then mean that the updates still minimize some J J that could be related to ℒ \mathcal{L} . This question is well-studied in the context of td learning [ 6 , 30 ] . Here, we provide a general result for functionals following the stopgrad regression principle. Theorem 2 (Conservativeness) . Assume the hypotheses of Theorem 1 hold for every f ∈ ℳ f\in\mathcal{M} , with ℳ \mathcal{M} a linear subspace of C 1 ∩ H C^{1}\cap H and T T Gateaux differentiable along ℳ \mathcal{M} , and write T ⁡ [ f ] T[f] for T ⁡ [ f , 𝔼 [ 𝐲 | 𝐱 ] ] T[f,\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[\mathbf{y}~|~\mathbf{x}]] . Suppose the semi-gradient g ⁡ [ f ] = f − T ⁡ [ f , 𝔼 [ 𝐲 | 𝐱 ] ] g[f]=f-T[f,\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[\mathbf{y}~|~\mathbf{x}]] is the gradient in ⟨ ⋅ , ⋅ ⟩ μ \langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mu} of a twice continuously differentiable scalar functional J : ℳ → ℝ J:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R} , meaning δ ​ J ​ [ f ; h ] = ⟨ g ⁡ [ f ] , h ⟩ μ \delta J[f;h]=\langle g[f],h\rangle_{\mu} for all f , h ∈ ℳ f,h\in\mathcal{M} (precise hypotheses in § E ). Then the Gateaux derivative D ​ T ​ [ f ] ​ h := d d ​ ϵ ​ T ​ [ f + ϵ ​ h ] | ϵ = 0 DT[f]\,h:=\frac{d}{d\epsilon}T[f+\epsilon h]\big|_{\epsilon=0} is symmetric with respect to ⟨ ⋅ , ⋅ ⟩ μ \langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mu} at every f ∈ ℳ f\in\mathcal{M} : ⟨ D ​ T ​ [ f ] ​ h 1 , h 2 ⟩ μ = ⟨ h 1 , D ​ T ​ [ f ] ​ h 2 ⟩ μ for all ​ h 1 , h 2 ∈ ℳ . \displaystyle\langle DT[f]\,h_{1},\,h_{2}\rangle_{\mu}=\langle h_{1},\,DT[f]\,h_{2}\rangle_{\mu}\qquad\text{for all }h_{1},h_{2}\in\mathcal{M}. The proof is in § E . Theorem 2 specializes the classical symmetry criterion for potential operators [ 44 , Theorem 5.1] to stopgrad regression. It gives a necessary condition for g g to be the gradient of some J J : when the condition fails, the semi-gradient g g has curl and is not the gradient of any scalar functional [ 3 ] . Corollary 6 . The semi-gradients of ℒ MF \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MF}} , ℒ iMF \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{iMF}} , ℒ LSD ​ - slim \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LSD\text{-}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\text{slim}}}} , and ℒ ESD ​ - slim \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESD\text{-}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\text{slim}}}} are not gradients of any twice continuously differentiable scalar functional J : ℳ → ℝ J:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R} in ⟨ ⋅ , ⋅ ⟩ μ \langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mu} (in the sense of Theorem 2 ). The proof in § E exhibits, for each objective, a base point f 0 f_{0} and two directions h 1 , h 2 ∈ ℳ h_{1},h_{2}\in\mathcal{M} at which D ​ T ​ [ f 0 ] DT[f_{0}] is not symmetric. In light of Corollary 6 , it is not a priori clear that following the semi-gradient field of MeanFlow, imf , slim- esd , or slim- lsd converges to the true flow map, which is the unique stationary point (Corollaries 2 – 5 ). Proposition 1 below shows that it does, by an explicit formula for the flow that does not rely on the uniqueness results.

sections.heading: 5.2 Convergence of functional semi-gradient flow for MeanFlow, improved MeanFlow, slim esd & lsd .
sections.text: In this section, we prove convergence results for functional semi-gradient flow for MeanFlow, improved MeanFlow, slim esd , and slim lsd objectives with stopgrad. We study MeanFlow directly, while for imf , slim esd and lsd , we consider distillation training following perfect flow-matching pretraining. This choice directly treats the matter of flow map convergence for a given velocity field, and aligns with the separation of flow matching pretraining and flow map post-training setup often used in practice. We succinctly state our setup and results here, and relegate full derivations and proofs to § G . We have shown that Theorem 1 applies to MeanFlow, imf , slim esd , and slim lsd , so that under the functional inner product ⟨ ⋅ , ⋅ ⟩ μ \langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mu} , the semi-gradient flow of each stopgrad term is ∂ τ f τ = − g ⁡ [ f τ ] \partial_{\tau}f_{\tau}=-g[f_{\tau}] , over optimization time τ \tau . For clarity of exposition, we choose a setting where g : ℳ → ℳ g:\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{M} , such that the semi-gradient flow on f ∈ ℳ f\in\mathcal{M} stays in ℳ \mathcal{M} . Under perfect flow-matching pretraining, the diagonal f τ ( t , t , ⋅ ) = v ( t , ⋅ ) f_{\tau}(t,t,\cdot)=v(t,\cdot) is invariant along the flow for slim esd and slim lsd (Lemma 5 ) and for imf . Hence, the flow matching terms in slim esd and slim lsd contribute no semi-gradient, and the imf flow coincides with the MeanFlow flow. We write the semi-gradient flow for the four objectives (eqs. 16 , 17 , 20 , 22 ), assuming perfect flow-matching pretraining for slim esd , slim lsd , and imf but not for MeanFlow (§ G.1 ). The Eulerian objectives (MeanFlow, imf , slim esd ) share an Eulerian semi-gradient flow, separate from the Lagrangian (slim lsd ) semi-gradient flow: Eulerian: ∂ τ F τ ( t , u , x ) \displaystyle\text{Eulerian:}\quad\partial_{\tau}F_{\tau}(t,u,x) = ( u − t ) ​ ( ∂ t F τ ​ ( t , u , x ) + ( ∂ x F τ ) ​ ( t , u , x ) ​ v ​ ( t , x ) ) \displaystyle=(u-t)\Big(\partial_{t}F_{\tau}(t,u,x)+(\partial_{x}F_{\tau})(t,u,x)\,v(t,x)\Big) (23) Lagrangian: ∂ τ F τ ( t , u , x ) \displaystyle\text{Lagrangian:}\quad\partial_{\tau}F_{\tau}(t,u,x) = − ( u − t ) ​ ( ∂ u F τ ​ ( t , u , x ) − v ⁡ ( u , F τ ​ ( t , u , x ) ) ) \displaystyle=-(u-t)\Big(\partial_{u}F_{\tau}(t,u,x)-v\bigl(u,F_{\tau}(t,u,x)\bigr)\Big) (24) We now give our main result: these functional semi-gradient flows converge to the true flow map. sections.heading: 6.1 Numerical semi-gradient flow experiments
sections.text: The result that F τ F_{\tau} has a closed-form expression in terms of F 0 F_{0} and F ∗ F^{*} is remarkable. We perform numerical experiments to check this by simulating functional semi-gradient flow on F τ F_{\tau} using equations 23 , 24 , and comparing this simulated F τ F_{\tau} to its theoretical value. We model F F on a discretized grid for ( t , u , x ) (t,u,x) in one to five spatial dimensions. See § I for further details. In Figure 3 left, we compare ‖ F τ ​ ( t , u , x ) ‖ 2 \|F_{\tau}(t,u,x)\|_{2} from simulation to the theoretical value from composing F ∗ F^{*} and F 0 F_{0} . We observe a Pearson correlation of 1.000000 over 220M points, indicating good numerical agreement with the theoretical relationship. In Figure 3 right, we plot the evolution of the pointwise error from the true flow map. We see excellent agreement between the dashed (theoretical) and solid (simulated) lines, further supporting the validity of the theoretical relationship. Right: Theoretical pointwise error to the true flow map (dashed) vs. simulated pointwise error (solid) in one spatial dimension. sections.heading: 6.2 Slim- esd and lsd : Stopgrad variants of Lagrangian and Eulerian self-distillation
sections.text: Theorem 1 motivated slim- esd , or slim- lsd , which modified stopgrad placements avoiding second-order derivatives. We train models on cifar-10 with slim- esd , or slim- lsd , and compare memory usage and performance to the original non-stopgrad ( esd , lsd ) and stopgrad objectives ( orig sg ) from Boffi et al. [9] . Each method is trained for 200k steps with checkpoints every 25k steps; for each sampling-step count we report the best EMA-model fid across checkpoints. We include more details in § K . The results are shown in Table 2 .

sections.heading: ImageNet Results.
sections.text: We train models on ImageNet with SD-VAE latents. We pretrain the MeanFlow-B4 model, a 90M diffusion transformer, with flow matching for 50k steps, then train with the full loss, and report one-step fid at 200k train steps (40 epochs). This setting compares objectives in shorter, ablation-style runs, with results in Table 3 . After FM-only pretraining, one-step fid is 315, showing that all objectives except for lsd improve fid while training. We find that slim lsd is competitive with lsd orig , and slim esd remains the best among esd variants.

sections.heading: 7 Related work
sections.text: Flow maps and consistency models. Flow maps and consistency models train networks to integrate probability-flow ODEs in few steps [ 40 , 41 , 28 , 21 , 37 , 8 , 36 ] . Many of these approaches use stopgrads to avoid backpropagating through model derivatives or nested model evaluations. We discuss the objectives of [ 9 ] and [ 15 ] in detail. Goldstein et al. [17] proved stationary-point results for SGFlow, a related stopgrad approach, but this approach still differentiates through forward-mode derivatives. In this work, we prove uniqueness of the true flow map as a stationary point for MeanFlow, improved MeanFlow, and our slim esd / lsd variants, and additionally prove convergence of functional semi-gradient flow for these methods. Stopgrads and semi-gradients. Semi-gradients have been studied extensively in rl [ 42 , 2 , 43 , 6 ] , where TD-style updates are not gradients of any fixed loss but nonetheless converge under conditions related to the structure of the Bellman operator and its fixed points [ 30 , 14 , 11 , 32 ] . Non-conservative update fields also arise in differentiable games such as gan s [ 3 , 24 ] . We derive our functional stopgrad formalism from first principles—perturbing only non-stopgrad occurrences of f f —and verify that it reduces to PyTorch’s detach in finite dimensions. The same construction is used in the context of fine-tuning and sampling in the proofs of adjoint matching and adjoint sampling [ 13 , 19 ] . Ponce et al. [33] studies two-player settings used in self-supervised methods such as byol ; there, stopgrads prevent model collapse for objectives whose minima would otherwise be collapsed solutions.

sections.heading: 8 Discussion
sections.text: We formalized the stopgrad operator in the calculus of variations, and proved a general theorem (Theorem 1 ) characterizing stationary points of stopgrad functionals. We analyzed stationary points and convergence for flow map objectives with stopgrad, and proposed slim stopgrad placements for lsd and esd that avoid differentiating through derivatives of f f , reducing training memory by 2 × 2\times . Looking forward, physics-informed neural networks (PINN) losses regress against pde residuals and share structural similarities with flow map objectives [ 18 ] . Our stopgrad regression principle may be used to propose stopgrad placements for pinn losses.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Our analysis is variational (infinite capacity, continuous optimization), so finite-width networks and stochastic gradient descent may behave differently. Our convergence results for imf , slim esd and slim lsd assume perfect flow-matching pretraining.

sections.text: Remark 1 (Standing regularity conditions) . All results on flow maps assume the following conditions: 1. sections.heading: Appendix C Uniqueness of stationary points for flow map objectives
Appendix D Unifying stopgrad objectives under the stopgrad regression principle
sections.text: In this section, we highlight the generality of the stopgrad regression principle by showing that it applies to stopgrad objectives not just for flow map training, but also for reinforcement learning and diffusion sampler training. Theorem 1 works with continuous, smooth functions and distribution μ \mu on inputs with full support. As such, we consider settings that match the presentation of Theorem 1 , such as continuous states, actions, and rewards in reinforcement learning.

sections.heading: Measure-valued targets
sections.text: In the reinforcement learning examples below, we use the random Dirac measure δ S t + 1 \delta_{S_{t+1}} on the random next state S t + 1 S_{t+1} in the target 𝐲 \mathbf{y} . The proof of Theorem 1 extends to such measure-valued targets because it only uses linearity of conditional expectations and affine dependence of T T on 𝐲 \mathbf{y} . sections.heading: Appendix G Proofs for convergence of functional semi-gradient flow
sections.text: For our convergence arguments, we choose for clarity of exposition to work in a functional analytic setting where g : ℳ → ℳ g:\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{M} , such that semi-gradient flow on f ∈ ℳ f\in\mathcal{M} stays in ℳ \mathcal{M} . This is more narrow than the functional analytic setting introduced in § 2 . Sufficient conditions for g : ℳ → ℳ g:\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{M} are: ℳ ⊂ C pol ∞ ∩ H \mathcal{M}\subset C^{\infty}_{\text{pol}}\cap H where C pol ∞ C^{\infty}_{\text{pol}} is the class of smooth functions such that every derivative has at most polynomial growth in x x uniformly over t , u t,u , and H H is L 2 ​ ( μ ) L^{2}(\mu) ; v ∈ C pol ∞ v\in C^{\infty}_{\text{pol}} and globally Lipschitz in x x uniformly in time, and μ \mu has all polynomial moments. These assumptions cover a broad class of flow maps and models of interest, such as linear interpolants between smooth positive data densities and a Gaussian base, and neural networks with activations with bounded derivatives. Nevertheless, g : ℳ → ℳ g:\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{M} is chosen for clarity of exposition: its assumptions are stricter than absolutely necessary for the convergence arguments, and could be weakened.

This transport equation, wherein a certain quantity is conserved over optimization time τ \tau , lets us characterize the semi-gradient flow evolution of the combined map, and then of the learned flow map. sections.heading: G.3 Exponential convergence rates under bounded derivatives.
sections.text: In this section, we prove that convergence occurs exponentially fast when the true velocity field has bounded derivatives. Before presenting the main proposition for exponential convergence, we first provide a lemma that we will use in the Lagrangian case. Lemma 6 . Suppose that the true velocity field v v is globally L L -Lipschitz in x x , uniformly in time (e.g., by the standing regularity conditions, Remark 1 ): ‖ v ⁡ ( s , x ) − v ⁡ ( s , y ) ‖ ≤ L ​ ‖ x − y ‖ for all ​ s ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] , x , y ∈ ℝ d . \|v(s,x)-v(s,y)\|\leq L\,\|x-y\|\qquad\text{for all }s\in[0,1],\ x,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. (85) Then the exact flow map F ∗ ( t , u , ⋅ ) F^{*}(t,u,\cdot) is e L ⁡ ( u − t ) e^{L(u-t)} -Lipschitz in its initial condition. Proof. Let y 1 , y 2 ∈ ℝ d y_{1},y_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , and consider two trajectories Z i ​ ( s ) := F ∗ ​ ( t , s , y i ) Z_{i}(s):=F^{*}(t,s,y_{i}) for i = 1 , 2 i=1,2 . By definition of the exact flow, each Z i Z_{i} solves d d ​ s ​ Z i ​ ( s ) = v ⁡ ( s , Z i ​ ( s ) ) \frac{d}{ds}Z_{i}(s)=v\bigl(s,Z_{i}(s)\bigr) with Z i ​ ( t ) = y i Z_{i}(t)=y_{i} . Subtract the two ODEs: d d ​ s ​ ( Z 1 ​ ( s ) − Z 2 ​ ( s ) ) = v ⁡ ( s , Z 1 ​ ( s ) ) − v ⁡ ( s , Z 2 ​ ( s ) ) . \frac{d}{ds}\bigl(Z_{1}(s)-Z_{2}(s)\bigr)=v\bigl(s,Z_{1}(s)\bigr)-v\bigl(s,Z_{2}(s)\bigr). Taking norms and using the global Lipschitz bound ( 85 ), d d ​ s ​ ‖ Z 1 ​ ( s ) − Z 2 ​ ( s ) ‖ ≤ L ​ ‖ Z 1 ​ ( s ) − Z 2 ​ ( s ) ‖ . \frac{d}{ds}\|Z_{1}(s)-Z_{2}(s)\|\leq L\,\|Z_{1}(s)-Z_{2}(s)\|. Grönwall’s inequality then yields ‖ Z 1 ​ ( u ) − Z 2 ​ ( u ) ‖ ≤ e L ⁡ ( u − t ) ​ ‖ Z 1 ​ ( t ) − Z 2 ​ ( t ) ‖ = e L ⁡ ( u − t ) ​ ‖ y 1 − y 2 ‖ . \|Z_{1}(u)-Z_{2}(u)\|\leq e^{L(u-t)}\|Z_{1}(t)-Z_{2}(t)\|=e^{L(u-t)}\|y_{1}-y_{2}\|. Since Z i ​ ( u ) = F ∗ ​ ( t , u , y i ) Z_{i}(u)=F^{*}(t,u,y_{i}) , we conclude that ‖ F ∗ ​ ( t , u , y 1 ) − F ∗ ​ ( t , u , y 2 ) ‖ ≤ e L ⁡ ( u − t ) ​ ‖ y 1 − y 2 ‖ . \|F^{*}(t,u,y_{1})-F^{*}(t,u,y_{2})\|\leq e^{L(u-t)}\|y_{1}-y_{2}\|. (86) ∎ Proposition 6 (Exponential convergence rates) . Assume the hypotheses of Proposition 1 . Assume in addition that the true velocity field v v is globally L L -Lipschitz in x x , uniformly in time, such that the exact flow map F ∗ ( t , u , ⋅ ) F^{*}(t,u,\cdot) is e L ⁡ ( u − t ) e^{L(u-t)} -Lipschitz in its initial condition. (a) Eulerian case (MeanFlow and simplified esd ). Assume M a := sup 0 ≤ t ≤ u ≤ 1 sup z ∈ ℝ d ‖ ∂ t a 0 ​ ( t , u , z ) ‖ < ∞ . M_{a}:=\sup_{0\leq t\leq u\leq 1}\sup_{z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\bigl\|\partial_{t}a_{0}(t,u,z)\bigr\|<\infty. (87) Then ‖ F τ ​ ( t , u , x ) − F ∗ ​ ( t , u , x ) ‖ ≤ M a ​ e − τ ​ ( u − t ) . \|F_{\tau}(t,u,x)-F^{*}(t,u,x)\|\leq M_{a}\,e^{-\tau}(u-t). (88) (b) Lagrangian case (simplified lsd ). Assume M b := sup 0 ≤ t ≤ u ≤ 1 sup x ∈ ℝ d ‖ ∂ u b 0 ​ ( t , u , x ) ‖ < ∞ . M_{b}:=\sup_{0\leq t\leq u\leq 1}\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\bigl\|\partial_{u}b_{0}(t,u,x)\bigr\|<\infty. (89) Then ‖ F τ ​ ( t , u , x ) − F ∗ ​ ( t , u , x ) ‖ ≤ e L ⁡ ( u − t ) ​ M b ​ e − τ ​ ( u − t ) . \|F_{\tau}(t,u,x)-F^{*}(t,u,x)\|\leq e^{L(u-t)}\,M_{b}\,e^{-\tau}(u-t). (90) Proof. We again treat the Eulerian and Lagrangian cases separately. (a) Eulerian case. By ( 75 ), a τ ​ ( t , u , z ) = a 0 ​ ( s t → u τ , u , z ) a_{\tau}(t,u,z)=a_{0}\bigl(s^{\tau}_{t{\shortrightarrow}u},u,z\bigr) . Also, a 0 ​ ( u , u , z ) = F 0 ​ ( u , u , F ∗ ​ ( 0 , u , z ) ) = F ∗ ​ ( 0 , u , z ) a_{0}(u,u,z)=F_{0}\bigl(u,u,F^{*}(0,u,z)\bigr)=F^{*}(0,u,z) , because every admissible flow-map parametrization satisfies F 0 ​ ( u , u , y ) = y F_{0}(u,u,y)=y . We now compare a τ ​ ( t , u , z ) a_{\tau}(t,u,z) and a 0 ​ ( u , u , z ) a_{0}(u,u,z) . The point is that, for fixed u u and z z , the map σ ↦ a 0 ​ ( σ , u , z ) \sigma\mapsto a_{0}(\sigma,u,z) is a C 1 C^{1} function of one real variable on the interval [ 0 , u ] [0,u] . Therefore the fundamental theorem of calculus gives a 0 ​ ( s t → u τ , u , z ) − a 0 ​ ( u , u , z ) \displaystyle a_{0}\bigl(s^{\tau}_{t{\shortrightarrow}u},u,z\bigr)-a_{0}(u,u,z) = − ∫ s t → u τ u ∂ 1 a 0 ( σ , u , z ) d σ . \displaystyle=-\int_{s^{\tau}_{t{\shortrightarrow}u}}^{u}\partial_{1}a_{0}(\sigma,u,z)\,d\sigma. (91) Taking norms and using the uniform bound ‖ ∂ t a 0 ​ ( t , u , z ) ‖ ≤ M a \|\partial_{t}a_{0}(t,u,z)\|\leq M_{a} , ‖ a τ ​ ( t , u , z ) − F ∗ ​ ( 0 , u , z ) ‖ \displaystyle\|a_{\tau}(t,u,z)-F^{*}(0,u,z)\| = ‖ a 0 ​ ( s t → u τ , u , z ) − a 0 ​ ( u , u , z ) ‖ \displaystyle=\bigl\|a_{0}\bigl(s^{\tau}_{t{\shortrightarrow}u},u,z\bigr)-a_{0}(u,u,z)\bigr\| ≤ ∫ s t → u τ u ‖ ∂ 1 a 0 ​ ( σ , u , z ) ‖ ​ 𝑑 σ \displaystyle\leq\int_{s^{\tau}_{t{\shortrightarrow}u}}^{u}\|\partial_{1}a_{0}(\sigma,u,z)\|\,d\sigma ≤ ∫ s t → u τ u M a ​ 𝑑 σ \displaystyle\leq\int_{s^{\tau}_{t{\shortrightarrow}u}}^{u}M_{a}\,d\sigma = M a ​ ( u − s t → u τ ) . \displaystyle=M_{a}\,\bigl(u-s^{\tau}_{t{\shortrightarrow}u}\bigr). (92) Using s t → u τ = u − e − τ ​ ( u − t ) s^{\tau}_{t{\shortrightarrow}u}=u-e^{-\tau}(u-t) , so u − s t → u τ = e − τ ​ ( u − t ) u-s^{\tau}_{t{\shortrightarrow}u}=e^{-\tau}(u-t) , we get: ‖ a τ ​ ( t , u , z ) − F ∗ ​ ( 0 , u , z ) ‖ ≤ M a ​ e − τ ​ ( u − t ) . \|a_{\tau}(t,u,z)-F^{*}(0,u,z)\|\leq M_{a}\,e^{-\tau}(u-t). (93) We now convert this bound back to the original ( t , u , x ) (t,u,x) -variables, by setting z = F ∗ ​ ( t , 0 , x ) z=F^{*}(t,0,x) . Since a τ a_{\tau} was defined by a τ ​ ( t , u , z ) = F τ ​ ( t , u , F ∗ ​ ( 0 , t , z ) ) , a_{\tau}(t,u,z)=F_{\tau}\bigl(t,u,F^{*}(0,t,z)\bigr), and since F ∗ ​ ( 0 , t , F ∗ ​ ( t , 0 , x ) ) = x F^{*}(0,t,F^{*}(t,0,x))=x , we obtain a τ ​ ( t , u , F ∗ ​ ( t , 0 , x ) ) = F τ ​ ( t , u , x ) a_{\tau}\bigl(t,u,F^{*}(t,0,x)\bigr)=F_{\tau}(t,u,x) . Similarly, F ∗ ​ ( 0 , u , F ∗ ​ ( t , 0 , x ) ) = F ∗ ​ ( t , u , x ) F^{*}(0,u,F^{*}(t,0,x))=F^{*}(t,u,x) by the semigroup property of the true flow. Therefore, ( 93 ) becomes ‖ F τ ​ ( t , u , x ) − F ∗ ​ ( t , u , x ) ‖ ≤ M a ​ e − τ ​ ( u − t ) , \|F_{\tau}(t,u,x)-F^{*}(t,u,x)\|\leq M_{a}\,e^{-\tau}(u-t), which is exactly ( 88 ). sections.heading: Appendix I Numerical experiments on convergence
sections.text: We numerically simulate functional semi-gradient flow from an initial F 0 F_{0} over optimization time τ \tau according to equations 23 , 24 . We compare the numerically simulated F τ F_{\tau} to its theoretical value from equations 25 and 26 . We model F F on a discretized tensor grid for ( t , u , x ) (t,u,x) , and compute ∂ t F , ∂ u F , ∂ x F \partial_{t}F,\partial_{u}F,\partial_{x}F using finite differences. These enable computing ∂ τ F τ \partial_{\tau}F_{\tau} . We use fourth-order Runge-Kutta to simulate the semi-gradient flow pde in τ \tau . At each step, we enforce the diagonal identity F τ ​ ( t , t , x ) = x F_{\tau}(t,t,x)=x exactly by overwriting elements in the tensor grid where t = u t=u . We perform experiments in 1 to 5 spatial dimensions, for 3 to 7 total dimensions, as grid discretization makes compute cost scale exponentially with the number of dimensions. Our experiments took seconds to minutes to run on one A100.

sections.heading: Velocity field.
sections.text: We use an affine velocity field: v ⁡ ( x ) = A ​ x + b v(x)=Ax+b , which allows the exact flow map F ∗ ​ ( t , u , x ) F^{*}(t,u,x) to be computed efficiently in closed form via a matrix exponential.

sections.heading: Data.
sections.text: We use the CIFAR-10 dataset [ 23 ] .

sections.heading: Architecture.
sections.text: We use the Song U-Net used in [ 15 ] . We use image resolution 32, in channels 3, out channels 3, model channels 18, num blocks 4, channel mult noise 2, resample filter [1,3,3,1], channel mult [2,2,2], encoder type standard, and decoder type standard.

sections.heading: Compute.
sections.text: We ran each experiment (a given method) for 200k gradient steps. To accomplish this, for each experiment we used 8x A100 GPUs. Each method was able to reach 200k steps with 96 hours of training.

sections.heading: Training Details.
sections.text: • Dataloading. We use pin-mem = True and 4 workers. • Time sampling. We use min times 1e-4 and max times 1 - 1e-4 for both training and sampling. We use probability t equals u set to 0.25. • EMA. We use EMA decay 0.9999. We start the EMA model at the 40k training steps model, and update once per gradient step thereafter. • Batch Size. We use batch size 64 per GPU and use 8 GPUs, meaning the effective batch size is 64*8=512. • Optimization. We use the AdamW optimizer with betas (0.9, 0.999). We use base learning rate 2e-4. We use linear warmup from 1e-6 up to the base learning rate for the first 20,000 steps. After warmup, the learning rate is constant at the base learning rate. • Seed. We use seed 0. • Velocity Warmup. We do not use any velocity warmup steps, similar to [ 15 ] and unlike [ 9 ] . • Dropout. We use dropout 0.20 • Adaptive Loss Weight. We use the adaptive loss reweighting from [ 15 ] with norm-p set to 0.75 and norm-eps set to 1e-3.

sections.heading: Evaluation Details.
sections.text: We evaluate FID from the non-EMA and EMA models every 25,000 steps. We evaluate this FID for several different sampling step counts per checkpoint, with number of function evaluations in {1,10,50,100}. We compute FID with the standard 50,000 samples using batch size 128. To compute FID, we use torchmetrics.image.fid.FrechetInceptionDistance .

sections.heading: K.2 ImageNet Experiments
sections.text: We use the B4 model from the meanflow-jax github repository which is a 90M diffusion transformer. We adopt their default settings, which uses patch size 4, learning rate of 0.0001, batch size 256, adam b2 of 0.95, and adaptive L2 weighting norm power of 1.0. We run flow-matching warmup for 10 epochs, and train for a total of 40 epochs. We use gradient surgery, prioritizing the diagonal gradient. Each run trained on 4x B200s, and training took about 8 hours.

Shen * Affiliation: Frontiers Research, Affiliation: Prescient Design, Genentech Mark Goldstein * Affiliation: Flatiron Institute Zichu Wang Affiliation: MIT Aahlad Puli Affiliation: NYU Rajesh Ranganath Affiliation: NYU Abstract Stopgrads are widely used in training machine learning models, but stopgrads can alter the gradient, stationary points and convergence guarantees of the original objective, which can make stopgrad training theoretically ungrounded. We introduce a stopgrad regression principle , which identifies a general template for stopgrad objectives with a closed-form characterization of stationary points and their uniqueness, unifying stopgrad objectives for flow maps, reinforcement learning, and diffusion samplers. We provide theoretical grounding for optimizing stopgrad flow map objectives by showing their unique stationary point is the true flow map, and showing positive convergence results for Eulerian and Lagrangian objectives, including MeanFlow and improved MeanFlow. Remarkably, we show that under functional semi-gradient flow, the learned flow map has a closed-form expression composing the initial flow map and the true flow map. We additionally use our stopgrad regression principle to propose modified stopgrad placements for flow map objectives which reduce training memory by 2 × 2	imes . 1 Introduction Stop gradients ( stopgrad ) are a basic primitive in automatic differentiation packages like PyTorch and JAX. Stopgrads leave the forward pass unchanged, but in the backward pass, they return a zero gradient and block further gradient propagation. Stopgrads are widely used in machine learning, including in self-referential objectives where a model is supervised in terms of itself, as in self-distillation, reinforcement learning ( rl ) [ 43 ] , consistency models and flow maps [ 40 , 15 ] , representation learning [ 33 ] , as well as variational inference [ 35 , 45 ] . For example, in rl , popular algorithms such as temporal-difference learning and actor-critic methods rely on stopgrads in practice [ 29 , 25 , 39 , 42 ] . However, stopgrad objectives update models with semi-gradients (differentiating only some occurrences of the model), which are not the gradient of the original objective [ 42 ] . Semi-gradient update fields may be non-conservative, meaning they may not be the gradient of any objective, and updates could follow a loop indefinitely without making progress. Whereas standard gradient descent is akin to marching through mountains and valleys, optimizing stopgrad objectives can be like wandering in Escher landscapes (Fig. 1 ). These concerns motivate understanding stopgrad optimization theory, which seeks to understand the stationary points and convergence of stopgrad objectives. Figure 1 : Gradient and non-gradient update fields. Left: Gradient fields are familiar valleys and mountains, while in stopgrad update fields, learning can make no progress and may not converge ( Relativity, M.C. Escher ). Right: (a) A well-behaved gradient field. (b, c) Non-gradient fields can result from stopgrads. While (b) still has a stable stationary point at the minimum, (c) has an unstable stationary point; small perturbations move trajectories away from the minimum and toward the limit cycle. In this work, we study a class of loss functions and stopgrad placements that yield update fields that converge to desired stationary points. Recently, stopgrads have featured prominently in methods for training flow maps , which learn to integrate probability-flow ODEs in few steps [ 40 , 41 , 28 , 21 , 37 , 8 , 36 ] . MeanFlow [ 15 ] introduced a stopgrad objective but did not analyze its stationary points or convergence. Boffi et al. [8] , Boffi et al. [9] introduced the Eulerian self-distillation ( esd ) and Lagrangian self-distillation ( lsd ) objectives and proposed specific stopgrad placements; they show the non-stopgrad loss has a unique minimum, but did not characterize the stationary points or convergence of the stopgrad variants. Despite the ubiquity and empirical utility of stopgrads, no general theoretical grounding exists for stopgrad objectives. This paper formalizes stopgrads via the calculus of variations (§ 2 ) and studies the stationary points and convergence of stopgrad objectives. Concretely, the paper makes the following contributions: ⋆ \star We introduce a stopgrad regression principle (§ 3 ), a general template for stopgrad objectives with a closed-form characterization of its stationary points as fixed points of the target operator. The template describes objectives where the learned model appears once outside the stopgrad, and regresses against targets that are affine in labels and stopgrad terms of the learned model. We also give a sufficient condition on the target operator under which a unique attainable minimizer of the ordinary (non-stopgrad) loss is the unique stationary point of the stopgrad loss, and we prove uniqueness directly for each flow map objective. The stopgrad regression principle is general, encompassing stopgrad objectives for flow maps, rl , and diffusion samplers [ 19 ] . The principle’s template is easy to check, so it assists in the design of new stopgrad objectives. ⋆ \star We apply the stopgrad regression principle to MeanFlow with stopgrad, and show that the true flow map is its unique stationary point , as desired. In contrast, removing the stopgrad removes the true flow map as a stationary point [ 8 ] , showing that the stopgrad in MeanFlow is necessary for principled optimization (§ 4.1 ). ⋆ \star We show that the true flow map is the unique stationary point of improved MeanFlow (§ 4.2 ). ⋆ \star We derive two new stopgrad objectives by introducing stopgrads in placements prescribed by the regression principle template in the ESD and LSD flow map objectives (§ 4.3 - 4.4 ), without changing the unique stationarity of the true flow map. We call these slim esd and lsd , as our stopgrads reduce training memory by 2 × 2	imes . Concurrent work has proposed equivalent objectives [ 22 , 34 ] , whereas we derive them in a principled manner from stopgrad optimization perspectives. We train flow maps and show that slim esd and lsd match or improve on Fréchet inception distance ( fid ) on cifar-10 and ImageNet . ⋆ \star We show positive convergence results for MeanFlow, Improved MeanFlow ( imf ) , slim esd , slim lsd (§ 5 ). We verify that their semi-gradients are not gradients of any objective, which raises questions on convergence. For slim esd , lsd , and imf , we study convergence of distillation training following perfect flow-matching pretraining, whereas we study MeanFlow training from scratch. Remarkably, we show that under functional semi-gradient flow, the learned flow map is a closed-form composition of the initial flow map and the true flow map , with “hand-off time” varying with optimization time (Fig. 2 ). Under standard assumptions, convergence occurs exponentially fast. Figure 2 : Convergence via closed-form composition (§ 5 ). Under functional semi-gradient flow, the learned flow map F τ F_{	au} at optimization time τ 	au is a composition of the initial F 0 F_{0} and the true flow map F ∗ F^{*} . As optimization time τ 	au passes, the “hand-off” time r τ r_{	au} interpolates towards u u for Eulerian and t t for Lagrangian, giving convergence to the true flow map. 2 Stopgrads in ML: from PyTorch to Proofs We formalize a mathematical definition of the stopgrad operator that is consistent with what is computed in practice. We start with stopgrads computed in programming libraries, move to directional derivatives, and then generalize to functional derivatives, which form the basis of our results. Stopgrads in practice Autodifferentiation frameworks such as PyTorch [ 31 ] and JAX [ 10 ] evaluate expressions in a forward pass, then compute parameter gradients in a backward pass via the chain rule. The stopgrad (or detach ) operation acts as the identity in the forward pass but returns a zero gradient in the backward pass. Let sg denote stopgrad as a mathematical operator. Taking the semi-gradient of the stop-gradient regression and applying a unit step yields f ← f − ( f − T ⁡ [ f , 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝐲 | 𝐱 ] ] ) = T ⁡ [ f , 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝐲 | 𝐱 ] ] f\;\leftarrow\;f-(f-T[f,\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}]])\;=\;T[f,\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}]] which is exactly fixed-point iteration of T T .
